changes.after: A command-line option is a named input given when a program starts. Reading an integer and checking its allowed range are separate steps.

before:
ARGV is the array of command-line argument strings. require "optparse" loads OptionParser; on("--minutes N", Integer) declares a value-bearing option and requests integer conversion. parse! consumes recognized options, leaving positional arguments in ARGV.

OptionParser.new returns the parser and supplies that parser to its construction block as options. Calls to options.on register rules on the same parser before parser.parse!(ARGV) processes the actual argument array.

For this example run ruby main.rb --minutes 15. A parsed integer can still be outside 1..60, and unexpected positional arguments are rejected. OptionParser::ParseError covers malformed or unknown options; neither option parsing nor shell quoting is permission to evaluate user text.

Complete local Ruby example; the app itself does not execute it:
```ruby
require "optparse"
minutes = nil
parser = OptionParser.new do |options|
  options.on("--minutes N", Integer) { |value| minutes = value }
end
begin
  parser.parse!(ARGV)
  if ARGV.empty? && minutes && (1..60).cover?(minutes)
    puts minutes
  else
    puts "invalid minutes"
  end
rescue OptionParser::ParseError
  puts "invalid option"
end

```
Expected output or behavior: 15. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Accept the parsed number only when it is from one through sixty.

Follow the labeled parts of this example.
```ruby
require "optparse"
minutes = nil
parser = OptionParser.new do |options|
  options.on("--minutes N", Integer) { |value| minutes = value }
end
begin
  parser.parse!(ARGV)
  if ARGV.empty? && minutes && (1..60).cover?(minutes)
    puts minutes
  else
    puts "invalid minutes"
  end
rescue OptionParser::ParseError
  puts "invalid option"
end
```
The output is `15`. The example starts with the minutes option set to fifteen.
Keep that input but narrow the allowed range to one through ten.
